title: Sogogi Muguk
subtitle: Beef and radish clear soup
excerpt: Thin slices of beef and cubed Korean radish are simmered together in a clean, lightly seasoned broth until the radish turns translucent and the beef is tender. This soup is a daily staple across Korean households. It takes around 40 minutes and is one of the most straightforward soups in the Korean repertoire.
sourceNotes: Sogogi muguk has been eaten in Korea for centuries as part of the everyday meal structure of rice, soup and banchan. The combination of beef and Korean radish is considered a classic pairing in Korean cuisine, with the radish becoming sweet and silky as it cooks in the beef broth.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze the soup without the spring onion garnish for up to 2 months. Reheat gently and add fresh spring onions when serving.
recipe.batchNotes: Double the quantities and store in portions. The soup keeps in the fridge for 3 days.

glossaryTerms.definition: Muguk is a Korean clear broth soup made with mu, the Korean radish. It is one of the most common everyday soups in Korean cooking, often made with beef or anchovy stock as the base. The radish turns translucent and mildly sweet as it simmers, absorbing the surrounding flavours. Muguk is served as part of the standard Korean meal alongside rice and banchan.

Mu is the Korean radish, similar to daikon in size and appearance but typically denser and slightly sweeter in flavour. It is white-fleshed and firm when raw, becoming tender and translucent when cooked. Korean radish is available in Asian supermarkets. If unavailable, daikon is the best substitute.

content.text: This recipe serves 4 and takes around 40 minutes including simmering time.

The key step is stir-frying the beef and radish briefly in sesame oil at the start. This draws out some of the beef fat and lightly caramelises the radish, adding depth to a broth that would otherwise rely entirely on simmering time. Do not skip this step even though it adds only a few minutes.
Heat the sesame oil in a large saucepan over a medium-high heat. Add the beef and radish and stir-fry for 2 to 3 minutes until the beef is no longer pink and the radish is lightly coated in the oil.
Add the garlic and stir for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Pour in the water and add the soy sauce. Bring to the boil, then reduce to a steady simmer.
Simmer for 20 to 25 minutes until the radish is completely tender and translucent. Skim any foam that rises to the surface in the first few minutes.
Add the gochugaru if using. Taste and season with salt. Add the spring onions in the final 2 minutes of cooking.
Ladle into bowls and serve hot alongside steamed rice.

items.symptom: Broth looks cloudy and murky rather than clear
items.cause: The soup was boiled hard rather than simmered, or the foam was not skimmed
items.fix: Keep the heat low enough for a gentle simmer. Skim any grey foam from the surface within the first 5 minutes of cooking. This makes a significant difference to the clarity of the final broth.

items.symptom: Radish is still firm after 25 minutes
items.cause: The radish was cut into pieces that were too large
items.fix: Cut the radish into cubes no larger than 2cm. Larger pieces need considerably more time. You can also test by pressing a piece against the side of the pot.

items.cause: Not enough beef relative to the water volume, or the initial stir-fry step was skipped
items.fix: Make sure to stir-fry the beef and radish first. If the broth still tastes weak, add another tablespoon of soy sauce and a pinch of salt. A small piece of dried anchovy added early also deepens the flavour.

content.text: Sogogi muguk is the kind of soup that appears on the Korean table without fanfare. It is cooked on a weeknight, served in a bowl alongside rice and a few small sides. It is restorative and light. Koreans often eat it when they are not feeling well or when they want something clean and simple after heavy food. The soup reheats well and is often better the next day.
